B's copy is fuller and has a stronger conversion CTA (free trial), and the 'not right for every need' honesty is on-brand. But it makes several unsupported claims and invents visuals, so it loses on truth.

Claims that the dashboard shows pages read and traffic sources on one page, and that it is 'deep custom reports' limited, are not in the confirmed facts.
The 'Same site. No banner.' mockup and the bar chart imply a visual comparison that is not backed by confirmed data.
'Your data stays yours' goes beyond the confirmed claim that it does not sell customer data.

reasons: B turns each fact into a reader benefit. It names the pain (clicking 'Accept all'), explains why a small script matters, and says what you still get. A states the fact and stops, so its posts are too thin to persuade in a Facebook feed.

B's call to action is a free trial, which matches the goal of more paying customers. A always sends people to the live demo, a softer step that is one click further from conversion.

A is more careful in its visual briefs (no mocked banners, no unconfirmed speed numbers). That caution is good, but it does not make up for flat copy that underuses confirmed proof.
truthX: The first comment says Plausible is 'built and hosted in the EU'. The confirmed facts only say EU-based; hosting comes from the insights, not the fact index.
truthY: 'No ad business behind us' goes beyond the confirmed facts. It is a reasonable inference but not stated.

The 'Same site. No banner.' mockup implies the whole site needs no banner. In truth only the analytics needs no banner, since the site may use other cookies. This is a mild risk of overclaiming.

The free version has the core self-care features. You complete small goals, reflections and breathing exercises, and your little bird earns energy for each one.

Finch Plus is an optional subscription that adds extra content and customization, for when you'd like more to explore and more ways to make Finch your own. It sits on top of the free version rather than replacing it.

Tap the link in bio to get Finch on iOS or Android, then find Finch Plus inside the app whenever you're curious.

reasons: A stays within the confirmed facts and is careful about the price: it says Plus is optional with extra content and customization, and it never invents a price or feature.

reasons: Both stay inside the confirmed facts: the pet-energy mechanic, the free core plus optional Finch Plus, and the 500k+ ratings at 5.0. Neither invents prices, features or results.

A's carousel is a save-worthy value piece. It offers four concrete tiny steps for a heavy day and ends on a screenshot-friendly summary slide. That is a proven Instagram mechanic, and it fits the highest-confidence audience: people who find self-care hard to start.

A's reel is tightly built. It has a concrete hook, one fact per beat, a looping end frame, burned-in captions and audio from Instagram's licensed business library. B's brief asks for a 'trending sound', which can be unavailable to business accounts.
A's production briefs are more usable for a non-expert. They require real screens only, no personal data, hands only and no mock screens.
B is warmer and more native in tone. It uses emojis, comment prompts and a gracious thank-you ratings post. B's reel also brings Finch Plus in more directly, which matches the subscriber goal.
B's captions and slides are more generic ('mountain to pebble', 'Your bird is waiting'). B's alt text summarizes the post instead of describing each slide.
A's captions lack engagement questions and read slightly stiff. That is why the margin is slight.
truthX: The first comment says the rating figure comes from the app store listing, and the reel films the store listing. The confirmed source is the site's displayed figure, so the store may show different numbers.
truthY: 'That part is free, and it always counts' implies a permanent free-tier promise that isn't confirmed.
The reel assumes a browsable in-app customization screen tied to Plus, which goes beyond the confirmed facts.

metaAds.primaryText: What happens during a furnace tune-up? Our tech checks airflow, reviews your controls and thermostat, cleans and adjusts key parts, and runs safety checks, especially on systems that have been running for years. It's the once-a-year visit that gets your system ready for long Iowa winter run times. Book online or call (515) 337-2456.

metaAds.audience: Homeowners within about 25 miles of Des Moines. Retarget visitors to the Bell Brothers heating pages from the last 30 days, plus a broad location-based audience.

metaAds.angle: Builds trust by showing exactly what the homeowner pays for, instead of a vague "tune-up special".
metaAds.creativeBrief: Film on a phone in a real customer home, with permission. Add captions for sound-off viewing. Show one step in the first 3 seconds. No claims about savings or breakdown prevention. End card: Schedule Online. Link to https://bellbrothers.com/heating/maintenance.

output.budgetNote:
- Cap: $1,500/month across both platforms, split about three-quarters Google, one-quarter Meta (assumption, adjust freely). Single days can run higher; the month stays capped.
- Google: one campaign, two ad groups (tune-up, replacement), phrase and exact only, Maximize clicks with a max CPC until bookings and calls are tracked.
- Clicks = daily budget divided by CPC. Pre-winter HVAC CPCs are assumed high (unverified, check in week 1), so expect only a handful of clicks a day.
- Meta: one ad set, three concepts, well under 50 results a week, so judge over 2-3 weeks. Not a special ad category.
- Rule: after 3 weeks, pause any ad group or concept above your target cost per booking; move its budget to the best performer.
- No results promised. Everything stays paused until you approve.

reasons: A stays almost entirely within the confirmed facts. Its copy is limited to 70+ years, weekend regular service, online scheduling, and installs of furnaces, heat pumps, boilers and mini-splits. It deliberately keeps weekend claims out of the replacement ad group.

A splits search into a tune-up ad group and a replacement ad group with cross-negatives. That fits the goal of booking both tune-ups and replacements, and it avoids the two groups competing with each other.

A's operational detail is strong: term exclusions, AI Max off with reasons, location presence settings, sitelinks, callouts, landing page checks, and a pause-and-reallocate rule. It is honest that CPCs are unverified and that no results are promised.
A's Meta ads use only confirmed facts, with a clear trust angle and a carousel that compares the four system types.

B has a good idea in the step-by-step tune-up video, but it relies on tune-up contents (airflow, controls, safety checks) and a gas/propane/oil claim that the confirmed facts don't support. That is a serious truth problem.
B's search plan covers only tune-ups, with no replacement ad group, even though the goal includes replacements. Its negative keyword list is thinner, and it puts a phone number in Meta primary text.
truthX: Structured snippet lists Geothermal and Thermostats, which are not in the confirmed facts.
Sitelink and carousel references to pages such as /reviews are assumed to exist.
The 'Local Des Moines Team' callout is mild extrapolation.
truthY: States that the tune-up checks airflow, reviews controls and thermostat, cleans and adjusts parts, and runs safety checks. None of this is in the confirmed facts and it comes only from an unverified landing page.
Claims Bell Brothers installs gas, propane and oil furnaces, which is invented.
Says 'now offers weekend appointments', implying a new offer.
'Furnace & Heat Pump Tune-Ups' and the 'heat pump tune up' keyword imply an unconfirmed service.
The ad copy says 'Iowa winter run times' and 'especially on systems that have been running for years', which are unsupported claims.
Audience age ranges (28-55 and 35-65) are arbitrary assumptions.

reasons: A covers both halves of the goal on Google: separate tune-up and replacement ad groups, with cross-negatives so each search reaches the right page. B runs only a tune-up search group. That ignores high-intent replacement searches, which are the most valuable jobs in this goal.

A stays disciplined on confirmed facts. It deliberately keeps weekend appointments out of replacement ads, because they are confirmed for regular service only. Its creative briefs also limit scripts to verified claims.

B leans on unconfirmed specifics. It names tune-up contents (airflow, controls, cleaning, safety checks), says it installs gas, propane and oil furnaces, and says Bell Brothers 'now offers' weekend appointments, implying they are new. None of these are in the confirmed facts.

A's account setup is more expert and more honest for a $1,500 budget: match types, AI Max off with reasons, term exclusions, location set to presence, a clear pause rule and no promised results. B's budget note is fine but thin.
B's Meta ideas are good native creative, especially the tune-up walkthrough video. They depend on unverified claims, though, and add arbitrary age bands that would narrow delivery for no reason.
truthX: The structured snippet lists Geothermal and Thermostats, which are not in the confirmed facts.
The 'Customer Reviews' sitelink with 'Read what neighbors say' assumes a reviews page and reviews that have not been confirmed.
truthY: The tune-up contents (checks airflow, reviews controls and thermostat, cleans and adjusts parts, safety checks) are not confirmed facts.
'Installs gas, propane and oil furnaces' is unconfirmed.
'Now offers weekend appointments' implies a new service, which is unsupported.
'Help you pick the right fit for your home and budget' and 'catch small issues early' are implied benefits that have not been confirmed.

v0f.topIssue: All Google search spend goes to low-ticket tune-ups with no replacement or installation search campaign, even though replacements are an explicit, high-value goal; the copy also adds unconfirmed claims such as 'now offers' weekend service, gas/propane/oil furnace installs and tune-up checklist details.

v22.topIssue: The ads have no offer, price, review proof or urgency hook against rivals advertising upfront pricing, 1,000+ reviews and 24/7 service, so they rely on weekend booking and '70 years' alone. The plan also slips in unconfirmed items (Geothermal and Thermostats snippets, a 'what neighbors say' reviews sitelink, a specific phone number) and spreads about $375/month of Meta budget across three concepts.
